title: The names at the end
hookLine: He is Allah, the King, the Holy, Peace, the Faithful … the Creator, the Fashioner (59:22–24)

lines: HE IS ALLAH, HE IS ALLAH, HE IS ALLAH.
cards: Anyone who has written a birthday card for their mother knows the problem. One word won't do. Kind, but also stubborn.
Funny, and also the one who stayed up when you were sick. Every word catches one side and misses the rest, so the card turns into a list. Surah Al-Hashr ends with a list too.
Three verses, each beginning He is Allah, then names, one after another, eleven of them in the last two verses alone.

teach.h: THE KNOWER OF THE UNSEEN AND SEEN.
teach.b: Verse twenty-two: he is God, other than whom there is no god, the knower of the unseen and the seen, the Merciful, the Compassionate.
Verse twenty-three, in Pickthall: "He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord, the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Majestic, the Compeller, the Superb."
In Arabic: al-Malik, al-Quddus, as-Salam, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-'Aziz, al-Jabbar, al-Mutakabbir.
Eight names in one breath. Then verse twenty-four: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. His are the most beautiful names." Al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir.
Commentators read these three as stages of making: al-Khaliq determines and plans, al-Bari' brings into being, al-Musawwir gives each thing its form.

teach.h: HIS ARE THE MOST BEAUTIFUL NAMES.
teach.b: Then the phrase for the whole idea: lahul-asma'ul-husna, his are the most beautiful names. And the surah ends where it began: everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies him.
A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says God has ninety-nine names, and whoever learns and keeps them enters paradise.
The familiar list of ninety-nine comes from a report in Tirmidhi, and many scholars think narrators gathered that list rather than the Prophet ﷺ speaking it himself.
But the names in these three verses are straight from the Qur'an, and many Muslims know them by heart. No single name says it all. That's why there are so many.

how: Many Muslims recite the last three verses of Surah Al-Hashr, especially morning and evening, and learn the names of God, often from the list of ninety-nine, as a form of remembrance.

o: the list of ninety-nine names in Tirmidhi
a single name of God meaning the Most Merciful
the surah that closes with many names for God

games.q: the names at the end — tap the pairs.

s: verse twenty-three lists eight names in a row
every scholar holds that the list of ninety-nine was spoken word for word by the Prophet
many think the familiar list in Tirmidhi was gathered by narrators.
the surah ends as it began, with everything glorifying God
its first and last verses say all in the heavens and earth glorify him.

games.q: you have three names: al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir. how do commentators tell them apart?
o: they're three ways of saying the same thing.
planner, maker, shaper: stages of making.
creator of heaven, earth and sea.
games.why: many commentators read them as stages: determining, bringing into being, and giving form.

practice: If you pray, recite the names of verse twenty-three slowly, one per breath: al-Malik, al-Quddus, as-Salam, al-Mu'min, and on, letting each settle before the next.
If that isn't yours, take three of the English words, Peace, the Holy, the Fashioner, and let one sit on each out-breath. Notice which one stays with you.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hashr, the surah that closes with name after name for God: eight in one breath, then planner, maker, shaper, and the most beautiful names. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: his are the most beautiful names. al-asma' al-husna is the phrase Muslims use for the names of God.

carryVoice: Your line: his are the beautiful names. One word was never going to be enough. That's day six hundred twenty-one.
